hook_text: Push 10 centimetres in, get 2 centimetres out. Not a loss. The missing 8 centimetres became force.
clip_script: Water does not squash, so area times distance in equals area times distance out. Master 2 square centimetres pushed 10: that is 20 cubic centimetres. Slave 10 square centimetres: 20 over 10, it moves 2. Five times the area, a fifth of the distance. Swap them and the small one flies out 50. Double a diameter and the area is four times, not two, so the distance drops to a quarter. Now add Pascal: force goes up by the area ratio while distance goes down by the same ratio. Force times distance stays the same. Mechanical advantage is slave area over master area. Above 1, strong and slow, the jack. Below 1, fast and weak, the digger's reach. Never both. You choose the ratio, and you pay in distance.
visual_style: Whiteboard two cylinders with a shaded water block sliding across and changing shape; the equation area times distance written both sides; a seesaw icon labelled force and distance.
mood: Neat arithmetic with a satisfying conservation payoff.
pacing: Volume rule, worked example, diameter trap, Pascal joins in, MA three cases.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and calculate how many pumps a 50 to 1 jack needs for a 10 centimetre lift.
